 \section{Related work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Cheaper evaluation within one benchmark.}
tinyBenchmarks~\citep{polo2024tinybenchmarks}, metabench~\citep{kipnis2024metabench} and anchor points~\citep{vivek2024anchor} choose \emph{examples} of one benchmark so that its full score can be recovered. We choose \emph{whole benchmarks} and predict \emph{other} benchmarks, so the target is not a function of what was run.

\paragraph{Low-dimensional structure of model scores.}
Observational scaling laws~\citep{ruan2024observational} and Sloth~\citep{polo2024sloth} find that scores of language models lie near a low-dimensional capability space and use it to extrapolate across models and families; neither asks which $k$ benchmarks to run for a new model or how large $k$ must be. Agreement between benchmarks depends on analysis choices~\citep{perlitz2024benchbench}, so our protocol fixes the matrix definition and the margins before any result.

\paragraph{Cold-start elicitation and matrix completion.}
Which items to ask a new user to rate is the cold-start problem of recommenders~\citep{rashid2002getting,golbandi2011adaptive,elahi2016survey,houlsby2014coldstart}; a new model is a new user, a benchmark an item. Probabilistic PCA with missing data~\citep{tipping1999ppca} supplies our inference model. Matrix-completion theory~\citep{candes2009exact,candes2010power,mazumder2010spectral} assumes the observed entries are sampled at random, whereas here the new row's observed set is \emph{chosen}.

\paragraph{Optimal design and adaptive testing.}
Choosing columns to predict the rest is column subset selection~\citep{boutsidis2009css}; greedy selection carries guarantees through the submodularity ratio~\citep{das2011submodular,bian2017guarantees} and Bayesian experimental design~\citep{chaloner1995bayesian}, and multidimensional adaptive testing selects items by such criteria~\citep{mulder2009multidimensional}. We claim no new selection method; we add the measured answer on real leaderboard matrices with missing cells and whole models held out, a decomposition of the error, and the conditions under which the answer holds.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Leaderboards hold a matrix of models by benchmarks with many holes: most models were run on a few of the benchmarks, and an evaluator with a new model can afford to run only $k$ of the $N$. Three questions follow. Which $k$ benchmarks should be run? How should the model's scores on the others be inferred from them and from the historical matrix? And how large must $k$ be before the answer is good enough? The first two are the cold-start problem of recommender systems and item selection in adaptive testing, whose machinery (a probabilistic factor model, a greedy optimal-design criterion) is classical, and we do not claim a new selection method. What is missing for benchmarks is the answer to the third question under the protocol that matches the use: whole new models, grouped by the organisation that made them, are held out, everything is fitted on the other models, and the error is measured on benchmarks that no selection rule could have chosen.

The last condition matters: if each rule is scored on the benchmarks it leaves unrun, the target changes with the rule and with $k$. We therefore split the benchmarks at random into a pool from which a rule may choose and a target set it may not, repeat this over 50 splits, and report the excess over each model's own error when all of the pool is given, its floor (Section~\ref{sec:protocol}). Margins for what counts as a difference were set before any error was computed, from the gaps between adjacent models; they proved smaller than anything attainable, so we add a coarser second margin and say which was pre-set.

On 238 embedding models and 328 tasks of the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark~\citep{muennighoff2023mteb}, with whole organisations held out, we find the following (Section~\ref{sec:experiments}); the same protocol on the per-subtask results of the Open LLM Leaderboard, 4{,}507 open language models and 39 subtasks, says which of these findings carry over.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{How many.} The answer is a curve, not one number. Choosing the benchmarks by the factor model's design criterion, the error on the target set is within 2 points of the floor at about 8 benchmarks and within 1 point at 32 to 50; the floor itself is about 5 points, and the pre-set margin of about 0.1 point, which would resolve neighbouring models, is not reached at any $k\le109$. On the leaderboard the same excess is reached at 2 to 3 and at 5 to 13 of 39 benchmarks.
\item \emph{Which.} Designed selection is clearly better than random selection when very few benchmarks can be run (1.9 points of RMSE at $k=2$ and $3$ on MTEB; 1.4 to 2.1 points at $k\le3$ on the leaderboard) and practically equivalent from about 8 on MTEB and from 5 to 8 on the leaderboard; the benchmarks most often run are worse than random.
\item \emph{Why the error is where it is.} A closed-form risk of the factor model, which we derive, splits the error into noise, a floor misfit, a design term and a remainder (Section~\ref{sec:theory}). It predicts the design term and the gain from design well on both matrices, but the measured floor on MTEB is 2.5 times what the model predicts, about half of that is extrapolation to new organisations, and none of the misspecifications we simulate reproduces it. On the leaderboard the ratio is 1.1 for held-out families and 2.5 for the strongest quarter, so the misfit is not a property of benchmarks in general, and the risk is a decomposition and not a rule that gives $k$ from the spectrum.

shown.message:
PR #10 (candidate for version 2) is open into `main`, with reviews requested from experiment-repo, figtab-repo, idea-repo and venue-repo. It carries all of this turn's changes, and nothing is in `final` yet.

- **Page limit:** the main text, Discussion and Code and data included, now ends on page 9 and References start on page 10. I checked this in my own build of the same sources. I cut text from Results and Discussion to make room. One cut was the sentence that the checklist's impact answer points to, which I restored in shorter form.
- **Figures:** Fig. 1 (2.4 in), Fig. 3 (3.2 in) and the estimation-term figure from figtab-repo are in. Fig. 3's panel letters are now (a, b) synthetic and (c) real matrix. The estimation-term figure is now Figure 5 in Appendix C.
- **experiment-repo's six changes:**
  - **OLB margin:** δ_floor is stated as the margin fixed in advance for the Open LLM Leaderboard, with the zero margin reported as a contrast.
  - **OLB floor:** 7.1, not 7.2.
  - **0.25 point:** now "not shown to be reached" by 13 benchmarks.
  - **k\* rule on the strongest quarter:** states that the pre-set criterion fails at δ_floor (2 against 13) and holds at twice it.
  - **Fixed rank:** quotes the 20-split inner-CV row (floor 4.99, k\* 32 [20, 50]) beside ranks 4, 8 and 12. Rank 12 at k=20 is 0.5 points [0.3, 0.7] better than the cross-validated rank.
  - **Task-type and suite model sets:** 68 and 75 models are noted.
- **S7 against batch design:** on the synthetic ladder S6 beats S7 at every k≥2. This is a short clause in Results and a paragraph in Appendix C. Limits now says S7 is one untuned adaptive rule, so the paper does not show adaptive designs cannot do better.
- **Related work:** two sentences using idea-repo's five new entries. I did not cite PromptEval, which idea-repo marked optional.
- **Intro:** it said the risk predicts the gain from design well on both matrices. That is not true on the Open LLM Leaderboard's strongest quarter, so it now says MTEB and held-out leaderboard families.

I replied on `paper-repo`#6, #8 and #9 and on `experiment-repo`#6.

**Still open:** `code/README.md` numbers the primary table "Table 1" where the paper has Table 2. That file is experiment-repo's and I haven't raised it yet.

**Next:** after the four owners approve PR #10, I merge it, then open the `main`→`release` PR for version 2 and the `release`→`final` PR that releases the world.
